info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 11.1: Aligning Translation Sentences and Authoring Interlinear Glosses by Hand.

name.text: 01 Question: Why Align Texts in a Digital Edition?

questiontext.text: Why is digital translation alignment superior to traditional facing-page print layouts?

generalfeedback.text: Digital alignment replaces guesswork with explicit links, connecting historical sentences directly to their modern translations.

answer.text: It creates explicit, machine-readable links connecting historical sentences directly to their modern translations.

feedback.text: Correct. Digital alignment eliminates guesswork by providing clickable, explicit connections between source sentences and modern translations.

answer.text: It automatically translates historical documents into modern slang without human oversight.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Alignment links verified human translations to their historical sources rather than generating unverified slang.

answer.text: It deletes the original historical language so readers only see modern English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital editions preserve both the original historical witness and the translation side by side.

answer.text: It converts all manuscripts into physical paper facsimiles to avoid digital screens.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Alignment is a computational method designed specifically for digital reading environments.

name.text: 02 Question: What is a Parallel Bitext? Interlingual vs. Intralingual Pairs

questiontext.text: How does an intralingual bitext differ from an interlingual bitext in digital historical editions?

generalfeedback.text: A parallel bitext links a historical source text to an authored target text, whether interlingual (across languages) or intralingual (across historical registers).

answer.text: An intralingual bitext pairs historical or dialectal prose with a modern rendering in the same language.

feedback.text: Correct. Intralingual alignment links two registers of one language (such as 1752 legal English to plain modern English), whereas interlingual alignment crosses languages.

answer.text: An intralingual bitext deletes all historical spelling and keeps only a single unlinked reading version.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A bitext always preserves both source and target texts as separate linked streams.

answer.text: An intralingual bitext translates across two separate national languages, such as French into English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Crossing between two distinct languages defines an interlingual bitext, not an intralingual one.

answer.text: An intralingual bitext merges every translation word directly inside the manuscript XML text stream.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both interlingual and intralingual bitexts preserve clean source files via standoff linking.

name.text: 03 Question: Step 0: Producing Your Target Text & Split-Editor Setup

questiontext.text: Before encoding standoff alignment links in VS Code, what Step 0 deliverable must you produce first?

generalfeedback.text: Alignment begins by drafting a separate target text file (target_translation.xml), then opening source and target side by side in VS Code's two-column split editor.

answer.text: A separate TEI target file (target_translation.xml) containing your authored ten-sentence rendering.

feedback.text: Correct. You must author your target text in target_translation.xml first, then open it beside the source in VS Code Two Columns (Cmd+\ / Ctrl+\).

answer.text: A merged single-file manuscript where modern English translations are pasted inside each French tag.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Mixing translations inside the source manuscript corrupts the XML witness.

answer.text: An automated neural network script that generates unreviewed translations without human comparison.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tuesday establishes a human-authored target text and manual alignment baseline.

answer.text: A printed paper copy of the archive catalogue showing only physical dimensions and watermarks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You need a digital target text in VS Code to align sentences side by side.

name.text: 04 Question: Sentences as Meaningful Units

questiontext.text: Which standard TEI XML element is used to mark sentence boundaries for translation alignment?

generalfeedback.text: Sentences marked with <s> tags provide the fundamental grammatical building blocks for sentence-level alignment.

answer.text: The <s> element, which wraps a complete grammatical sentence.

feedback.text: Correct. The TEI <s> tag denotes a sentence unit, providing a clean target for sentence-level alignment.

answer.text: The <body> tag, which marks the entire document text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <body> contains the entire main text, not individual sentences.

answer.text: The <gap> tag, which indicates missing or illegible text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <gap> records lacunae or damage, not sentence boundaries.

answer.text: The <title> tag, which gives the title of the work.

feedback.text: Incorrect. <title> is for bibliographic titles, not running text sentences.

name.text: 05 Question: Assigning Unique Identifiers (xml:id)

questiontext.text: Why must every sentence in an alignment project receive a unique xml:id attribute?

generalfeedback.text: Every sentence receives a unique xml:id attribute so that external link elements can point to it without ambiguity.

answer.text: To give each sentence a unique digital address so external link elements can connect them without ambiguity.

feedback.text: Correct. Unique xml:id attributes act like postal addresses, allowing link elements to pair specific sentences.

answer.text: To change the font color of the sentence to bright green in the web browser.

feedback.text: Incorrect. xml:id is an identifier attribute, not a visual styling rule.

answer.text: To translate French words into English automatically without human review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. xml:id only identifies elements; it does not perform language translation.

answer.text: To lock the file so that no other student can open it on their computer.

feedback.text: Incorrect. xml:id does not encrypt or password-protect files.

name.text: 06 Question: One-to-One Correspondences (1:1)

questiontext.text: What is a one-to-one (1:1) sentence alignment?

generalfeedback.text: A one-to-one alignment occurs when a single source sentence maps directly onto a single translated sentence.

answer.text: An alignment where exactly one source sentence maps directly onto a single translated sentence.

feedback.text: Correct. A 1:1 alignment pairs a single source sentence (such as s1) with a single target sentence (such as t1).

answer.text: An alignment where one word in language A translates to ten words in language B.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That describes lexical expansion, not sentence-level 1:1 alignment.

answer.text: An alignment where an entire book is summarized into a single sentence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is an abstract or summary, not a sentence alignment.

answer.text: An alignment where every vowel is replaced by the number 1.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Alignment links semantic and grammatical units, not character substitutions.

name.text: 07 Question: One-to-Many Alignments (1:N)

questiontext.text: When does an editor create a one-to-many (1:N) alignment?

generalfeedback.text: A one-to-many alignment connects a single complex source sentence to multiple shorter modern translated sentences.

answer.text: When a single complex historical source sentence is split into multiple shorter modern sentences in the translation.

feedback.text: Correct. A 1:N alignment connects one long source sentence (e.g. s4) to multiple translated sentences (e.g. t4 and t5).

answer.text: When an editor translates a document into twenty different European languages at once.

feedback.text: Incorrect. 1:N refers to the ratio of source sentences to target sentences within a single translation.

answer.text: When a manuscript page has multiple physical ink stains.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Physical stains are codicological defects, not translational sentence splits.

answer.text: When an entire paragraph is accidentally erased from the translation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Omission is a 1:0 alignment, not a 1:N alignment.

name.text: 08 Question: Many-to-One Alignments (N:1)

questiontext.text: What occurs during a many-to-one (N:1) alignment?

generalfeedback.text: A many-to-one alignment links multiple concise source sentences to a single combined translation sentence.

answer.text: Multiple concise historical source sentences are combined into a single flowing translated sentence.

feedback.text: Correct. In an N:1 alignment, several short source sentences (e.g. s8 and s9) map onto a single combined translation sentence (t8).

answer.text: A translator expands a single English word into five French paragraphs.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would be a massive expansion, not a many-to-one sentence combination.

answer.text: Multiple scribes copy the same document simultaneously in different rooms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That describes historical scriptorium production, not text alignment.

answer.text: A student submits multiple identical homework assignments to Moodle.

feedback.text: Incorrect. N:1 alignment relates to grammatical sentence correspondence.

name.text: 09 Question: Omissions and Additions (1:0 and 0:1)

questiontext.text: How does a digital alignment record an omission where a historical sentence was left untranslated?

generalfeedback.text: Textual asymmetries include omissions (1:0) and additions (0:1), where sentences exist in only one language.

answer.text: By leaving the source sentence unlinked or explicitly directing its target pointer to #none.

feedback.text: Correct. Recording omissions as 1:0 alignments (or pointing to #none) documents that the source sentence has no translation.

answer.text: By inventing a fake English sentence and pretending the historical author wrote it.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly ethics prohibit fabricating translations.

answer.text: By deleting the historical sentence from the original manuscript XML file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You must never delete historical text to hide translation discrepancies.

answer.text: By crashing the computer so the XML file cannot be saved.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Alignment standards cleanly handle omissions without errors.

name.text: 10 Question: Inline Markup vs. Standoff Markup

questiontext.text: Why does the TEI community strongly recommend standoff markup over inline markup for translation alignment?

generalfeedback.text: Standoff markup stores alignment links separately from text content, keeping both original and translation files clean and valid.

answer.text: Standoff markup keeps source and translation files clean and independent, preventing modern words from cluttering historical text.

feedback.text: Correct. Standoff markup stores links in a separate block, preserving the layout and schema validity of both text streams.

answer.text: Inline markup is forbidden by international copyright law in Canada.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Markup architecture is a technical design choice, not a copyright statute.

answer.text: Standoff markup makes XML files run ten times faster on old laptops.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standoff markup is chosen for structural clarity and modularity, not raw CPU speed.

answer.text: Inline markup converts all XML tags into capital letters automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Inline markup simply embeds notes directly within the text stream.

name.text: 11 Question: The TEI Standoff Philosophy

questiontext.text: How does the TEI standoff architecture allow an edition to support multiple translations over time?

generalfeedback.text: The TEI standoff architecture separates text content from analytical links, allowing multiple translations without altering the base text.

answer.text: New translations can be added with their own link groups without modifying the original manuscript transcription.

feedback.text: Correct. Because links sit outside the text, you can add new translations (e.g. French, Mi'kmaw, German) without touching the source XML.

answer.text: It forces all translations to merge into a single gigantic paragraph.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standoff markup preserves distinct, modular text files.

answer.text: It requires the original manuscript to be destroyed once the translation is complete.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital editions aim to preserve historical manuscript witnesses indefinitely.

answer.text: It restricts the edition to exactly one English translation forever.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The main advantage of standoff architecture is that it easily accommodates multiple translations.

name.text: 12 Question: Introducing <linkGrp> and <link>

questiontext.text: In a TEI <link> element, what prefix must precede every xml:id listed in the @target attribute?

generalfeedback.text: The <link> element pairs sentence IDs using the @target attribute, prefixing each ID with a number sign (#).

answer.text: A number sign or hash symbol (#), which indicates an ID reference within the document.

feedback.text: Correct. The hash symbol (#s1 #t1) tells the XML processor to resolve the name as a local element ID.

answer.text: An exclamation point (!), which tells the parser to highlight the sentence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Exclamation marks are not the standard XML ID pointer prefix.

answer.text: A dollar sign ($), which marks currency in 18th-century treaties.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hash marks (#) are used for ID references in TEI and HTML.

answer.text: An ampersand (&), which creates an XML character entity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ampersands escape entities; URI ID references require a hash mark.

name.text: 13 Question: Placing the <linkGrp> in the TEI Document

questiontext.text: Where is the standard location for a <linkGrp> element inside a TEI document?

generalfeedback.text: Place your <linkGrp> elements inside a <standOff> element at the end of your TEI document for clean organization.

answer.text: Inside a dedicated <standOff> element, or within a <div type="alignments"> in <back>.

feedback.text: Correct. TEI P5 provides the <standOff> element (or back matter divs) specifically to hold external link groups.

answer.text: Inside the <titleStmt> of the <teiHeader> before the author name.

feedback.text: Incorrect. titleStmt contains metadata about the edition title, not text alignment links.

answer.text: Inside a <graphic> element embedded in the banner image.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Graphic elements link image URLs, not parallel text alignments.

answer.text: Scattered randomly between words in the manuscript transcription.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That would defeat the entire purpose of standoff markup.

name.text: 14 Question: Validating Standoff Links in VS Code

questiontext.text: What is a common error when writing standoff links by hand in VS Code?

generalfeedback.text: Valid standoff links always include the # prefix and point directly to existing, unique xml:id attributes.

answer.text: Forgetting the hash mark (#) before an ID, writing target="s1 t1" instead of target="#s1 #t1".

feedback.text: Correct. Omitting the hash mark creates an invalid pointer that XML processors cannot resolve.

answer.text: Saving the file with the .xml file extension.

feedback.text: Incorrect. .xml is the correct and required file extension.

answer.text: Using lowercase letters for sentence IDs like s1 and t1.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lowercase letters are standard and valid in xml:id attributes.

answer.text: Leaving spaces between the target IDs inside the attribute quotes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Spaces are required to separate multiple IDs inside the @target attribute.

name.text: 15 Question: Moving from Sentences to Words: Why We Need Finer Detail

questiontext.text: Why do scholarly digital editions require word-level and morpheme-level analysis in addition to sentence alignment?

generalfeedback.text: While sentence alignment links general ideas, interlinear glossing exposes the exact grammatical mechanics of individual words.

answer.text: To analyze specific grammatical choices, terminology, and historical phrasing that sentence alignment cannot reveal.

feedback.text: Correct. While sentence alignment shows general meaning, interlinear glossing exposes the exact grammatical mechanics of individual words.

answer.text: To make the XML files as large as possible to consume hard drive storage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly markup aims for philological precision, not unnecessary file bloat.

answer.text: Because sentences are completely meaningless in historical linguistics.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Sentences are essential units, but word-level analysis provides deeper grammatical detail.

answer.text: To prevent students from reading the English translation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Interlinear glossing enhances reading comprehension by explaining every word component.

name.text: 16 Question: What is an Interlinear Gloss?

questiontext.text: What is an interlinear gloss in historical manuscript scholarship and linguistics?

generalfeedback.text: Interlinear glossing places grammatical and lexical explanations directly between text lines following standardized linguistic rules.

answer.text: A line of linguistic or lexical explanation written directly between the lines of a text.

feedback.text: Correct. Interlinear glosses place grammatical and translation notes between text lines, following rigorous linguistic conventions.

answer.text: A decorative border painted in gold leaf on the cover of a leather book.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is illumination or binding decoration, not an interlinear gloss.

answer.text: A footnote placed at the very end of a printed book in tiny six-point font.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Glosses sit between text lines (interlinear), not in endnotes.

answer.text: A list of books borrowed from a university library during study break.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That is a library circulation record.

name.text: 17 Question: The Leipzig Glossing Rules: An Overview

questiontext.text: What was the primary motivation behind the creation of the Leipzig Glossing Rules?

generalfeedback.text: The Leipzig Glossing Rules provide an international standard for formatting multilingual texts so their grammar is clear to any scholar.

answer.text: To establish an international standard so that any scholar can understand a text's grammar without needing to speak the language.

feedback.text: Correct. The Leipzig rules ensure worldwide transparency and consistency across multilingual linguistic editions.

answer.text: To force all historical documents to be translated into German.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The rules govern formatting and notation, not the target language.

answer.text: To ban English words from digital scholarly editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Leipzig rules work with any source and target languages.

answer.text: To make linguistic textbooks impossible for beginners to read.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The rules standardize notation specifically to make texts accessible and clear.

name.text: 18 Question: The Four-Tier Architecture of Leipzig Glossing

questiontext.text: What are the four vertical lines in a standard Leipzig interlinear gloss?

generalfeedback.text: The four-line Leipzig layout moves systematically from raw historical spelling to grammatical breakdown, linguistic labels, and modern translation.

answer.text: Line 1: Surface Text; Line 2: Morpheme Breakdown; Line 3: Grammar Gloss; Line 4: Free Translation.

feedback.text: Correct. The four tiers systematically move from historical spelling to morphemic segmentation, grammatical labels, and fluent translation.

answer.text: Line 1: English; Line 2: French; Line 3: Spanish; Line 4: German.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The tiers represent analytical linguistic layers, not four European languages.

answer.text: Line 1: Date; Line 2: Time; Line 3: Room; Line 4: Instructor.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are timetable metadata fields, not interlinear gloss tiers.

answer.text: Line 1: Title; Line 2: Paragraph; Line 3: Sentence; Line 4: Period.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are text structural levels, not Leipzig gloss lines.

name.text: 19 Question: Tier 1: The Historical Surface Text

questiontext.text: What should an editor do with historical spelling, accents, and punctuation in Line 1 of a Leipzig gloss?

generalfeedback.text: Line 1 preserves the raw historical spelling of the witness without modernization or silent alterations.

answer.text: Preserve the historical spelling and punctuation exactly as written in the manuscript witness.

feedback.text: Correct. Line 1 records the authentic historical surface text without modernization or silent alterations.

answer.text: Modernize all words to conform to standard 2026 Canadian English spelling.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Line 1 must preserve the witness; modern phrasing belongs in Line 4.

answer.text: Delete all accented letters because computers cannot display them.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern UTF-8 encoding fully supports all historical accented characters.

answer.text: Translate the words into Latin before typing them into Line 1.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Line 1 holds the primary language of the source artifact.

name.text: 20 Question: Tier 2: Word and Morpheme Segmentation

questiontext.text: What punctuation mark is used in Line 2 to separate words into their constituent morphemes (stems and endings)?

generalfeedback.text: Line 2 breaks complex words into stems and grammatical endings using hyphens to mark boundaries.

answer.text: A hyphen (-), which marks physical boundaries between prefixes, stems, and suffixes.

feedback.text: Correct. Hyphens in Line 2 separate distinct morphemic building blocks (e.g. décret-s).

answer.text: An asterisk (*), which denotes a reconstructed word in historical linguistics.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Asterisks mark unverified or reconstructed forms, not morpheme boundaries.

answer.text: An exclamation mark (!), which indicates an imperative command.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Exclamation marks are grammatical sentence punctuation.

answer.text: A plus sign (+), which is used only for mathematical addition.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Leipzig Rule 2 specifically designates the hyphen for morpheme cuts.

name.text: 21 Question: Tier 3: Grammatical Abbreviations

questiontext.text: In Line 3 of a Leipzig gloss, how are grammatical category labels visually distinguished from lexical meanings?

generalfeedback.text: Line 3 combines lowercase English meanings for word stems with standard uppercase abbreviations for grammatical endings.

answer.text: Grammatical labels are written in standard uppercase abbreviations (e.g. PL, PST), while lexical stems are written in lowercase English.

feedback.text: Correct. The Leipzig rules reserve capital letters for grammatical functions (PL, DEF, PST) and lowercase for word translations.

answer.text: Grammatical labels are written in red ink while word stems are written in blue ink.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Leipzig rules rely on case conventions (uppercase vs lowercase), not text color.

answer.text: Grammatical labels are enclosed in square brackets with smiley faces.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly standards avoid informal symbols.

answer.text: All words in Line 3 must be written entirely in Greek letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Line 3 uses standard Latin alphabet abbreviations.

name.text: 22 Question: The Hyphen vs. The Period: Rule 2 Explained

questiontext.text: According to Leipzig Rule 2, when should a period (.) be used between labels in Line 3 instead of a hyphen?

generalfeedback.text: Hyphens mark physical boundaries between distinct morphemes; periods join multiple grammatical concepts packed into a single ending.

answer.text: When a single indivisible morpheme expresses multiple grammatical meanings at the same time (e.g. speak-3SG.PST).

feedback.text: Correct. A period joins multiple grammatical labels that belong to a single fused ending that cannot be physically separated.

answer.text: Whenever an editor gets tired of typing hyphens.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Punctuation in Leipzig glosses has precise linguistic meanings.

answer.text: Only at the very end of the sentence to show it is finished.

feedback.text: Incorrect. That describes normal sentence punctuation; inside Line 3, periods join portmanteau categories.

answer.text: Whenever a word has more than ten letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Word length does not determine morphemic punctuation.

name.text: 23 Question: Tier 4: The Free Idiomatic Translation

questiontext.text: What is the formatting convention for Line 4 in a Leipzig interlinear gloss?

generalfeedback.text: Line 4 delivers a fluent, idiomatic English translation enclosed in quotation marks, conveying the complete meaning of the passage.

answer.text: It is a fluent, natural English translation enclosed in quotation marks.

feedback.text: Correct. Line 4 conveys the complete thought in idiomatic English, enclosed in double quotation marks.

answer.text: It is a word-for-word literal translation that ignores English grammar.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Word-for-word analysis belongs in Lines 2 and 3; Line 4 provides fluent idiomatic English.

answer.text: It must be written in rhyming poetry with exactly fourteen lines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Line 4 is a prose translation of the sentence.

answer.text: It should be left blank so the student can guess the meaning.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A complete four-line gloss always provides the translation on Line 4.

name.text: 24 Question: Case Study 1: French Revolutionary Decree (Ace's Document)

questiontext.text: When glossing Ace's 1791 French decree, why is the article l' glossed as DEF.SG with a period?

generalfeedback.text: Applying Leipzig rules to 18th-century French clarifies how gender, number, and verb conjugations function in legal proclamations.

answer.text: Because the single letter l' expresses both definite article status and singular number in one indivisible piece.

feedback.text: Correct. The single consonant conveys two grammatical categories simultaneously, so Leipzig Rule 2 requires a period between DEF and SG.

answer.text: Because the French printer made a typo on the printing press.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Elision of the article before a vowel is standard French grammar.

answer.text: Because the period indicates that the word is secret.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The period indicates combined grammatical features.

answer.text: Because French laws were forbidden from using hyphens in 1791.

feedback.text: Incorrect. French legal documents used standard orthography.

name.text: 25 Question: Case Study 2: Peace and Friendship Treaty of 1752 (Andromeda's Document)

questiontext.text: How does interlinear glossing help students analyze historical colonial treaties like the 1752 treaty?

generalfeedback.text: Glossing historical legal English highlights the precise function of modal verbs and passive agreements in colonial treaties.

answer.text: It isolates formal legal phrasing, obligations, and modal verbs like shall, revealing how agreements were structured.

feedback.text: Correct. Glossing legal terminology clarifies the exact grammatical mechanisms governing rights and obligations in historical treaties.

answer.text: It proves that colonial treaties were printed on modern laser printers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The 1752 treaty was printed on historical rag paper with movable type.

answer.text: It converts all treaty terms into Latin religious prayers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Glossing analyzes the actual legal language of the document.

answer.text: It deletes all references to historical dates and locations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Codicological and historical context is preserved throughout.

name.text: 26 Question: Case Study 3: Folk Art Correspondence (Olyvia's Document)

questiontext.text: Why is alignment and glossing valuable for Olyvia's 1967 Maud Lewis letters, even though they are written in English?

generalfeedback.text: Interlinear glossing and alignment help scholars document vernacular dialect, informal handwriting, and parallel French translations.

answer.text: It allows editors to align vernacular handwritten expressions with normalized reading texts or parallel French translations.

feedback.text: Correct. Alignment links informal vernacular handwriting to regularized reading editions and enables bilingual Canadian editions.

answer.text: Because Maud Lewis wrote her personal letters in ancient Classical Greek.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Maud Lewis wrote in 20th-century Maritime English.

answer.text: Because personal letters are not allowed in digital archives without complete translation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Letters are valuable primary sources that benefit from linguistic alignment.

answer.text: Because folk art can only be understood through computer algorithms.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital alignment supports human appreciation of folk art and personal writing.

name.text: 27 Question: Encoding Leipzig Glosses in TEI XML

questiontext.text: Which three TEI XML elements are typically used to represent words, morphemes, and glosses?

generalfeedback.text: TEI encodes interlinear glosses using <w> for words, <m> for morphemes, and <gloss> for linguistic definitions.

answer.text: <w> for words, <m> for morphemes, and <gloss> for grammatical definitions.

feedback.text: Correct. TEI provides <w>, <m>, and <gloss> specifically for fine-grained linguistic markup.

answer.text: <cat>, <dog>, and <bird>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are animal names, not valid TEI elements.

answer.text: <div>, <p>, and <lb/>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those represent larger structural layout units (sections, paragraphs, line breaks), not morphemes.

answer.text: <author>, <publisher>, and <date>.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Those are bibliographic metadata elements.

name.text: 28 Question: Common Novice Pitfalls in Manual Alignment

questiontext.text: What visual formatting problem occurs if you put three words in Line 1 but four gloss columns in Line 3?

generalfeedback.text: Common alignment mistakes include missing # hash prefixes, mismatched column counts, and improper use of hyphens versus periods.

answer.text: The columns become misaligned, destroying the vertical word-by-word correspondence.

feedback.text: Correct. Every word column in Line 1 must correspond exactly to one gloss column in Line 3 to preserve vertical alignment.

answer.text: The computer monitor will immediately turn off.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unbalanced columns cause a visual formatting error, not hardware failure.

answer.text: The text will automatically convert into a PDF notes file.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Mismatched columns break the layout; they do not trigger automated compilation.

answer.text: The French words will be replaced by Latin numbers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Text tokens remain unchanged, but the alignment columns become shifted.

name.text: 29 Question: Creating Your Tuesday Ground Truth Files

questiontext.text: Which three manual deliverables in your project folder form Tuesday's verified human ground truth?

generalfeedback.text: Your Tuesday manual files establish the verified human ground truth against which all algorithmic and AI tools will be measured.

answer.text: target_translation.xml (target text), alignment_manual.xml (linkGrp), and gloss_manual.xml (3 glosses).

feedback.text: Correct. Together, your authored target text, standoff sentence alignments, and three Leipzig glosses form Tuesday's human benchmark.

answer.text: Three temporary scratch backups meant to be deleted immediately once the Wednesday lab session starts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. These files are permanent course deliverables used to benchmark the rest of the week's work.

answer.text: A single unlinked PDF printout, a raw camera photograph, and a blank repository configuration script.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tuesday's deliverables are structured TEI XML files for your target text, sentence links, and glosses.

answer.text: An automated AI summary, a compiled HTML slide presentation, and an unverified library call-number log.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tuesday is the manual baseline authored by human judgment before Wednesday and Friday tools.

name.text: 30 Question: Looking Ahead: Why Today's Manual Work Matters

questiontext.text: How will you use today's manual alignment work during tomorrow's deterministic class meeting?

generalfeedback.text: Today's manual alignment provides the essential benchmark required to test and audit automated and AI-assisted tools for the rest of the week.

answer.text: You will test whether an automated alignment algorithm can match the sentence connections you created by hand.

feedback.text: Correct. Tomorrow's automated tools will be audited directly against the human gold standard you created today.

answer.text: You will discard your work and let the computer start over from scratch.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The computer output is measured against your manual ground truth.

answer.text: You will manually calculate statistical matrix multiplications on a chalkboard.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You will use automated tools to test against your manual baseline.

answer.text: You will switch to a completely different language and abandon your manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. You continue working with your chosen primary document.
